boxes.title: BEFORE WE BEGIN
boxes.body: Before we begin, it's important to understand the foundation this lesson in quantum computing is built on: how a qubit's state is written down, and why we picture it the way we do. Let's build it up one piece at a time.

boxes.title: WHERE A QUBIT LIVES
boxes.body: ℂ² ("C two") is where a qubit's state lives. The ℂ stands for the complex numbers, and the ² means a pair of them. So a qubit's state is described by two complex numbers.

boxes.title: WRITING A QUBIT'S STATE
boxes.body: We write a qubit's state |ψ⟩ ("psi") as a column of those two numbers, α ("alpha") and β ("beta"). α belongs to |0⟩ and β belongs to |1⟩: together they say how much of each the qubit holds.

boxes.title: COMPLEX NUMBERS
boxes.body: Each of α and β is a complex number: a real part plus an imaginary part. In α = a + b<color=#FFE14D>i</color>, a and b are ordinary real numbers, like 0.6 or −2. The same goes for c and d in β.

boxes.title: THE IMAGINARY UNIT
boxes.body: The <color=#FFE14D>i</color> is the imaginary unit: the number whose square is −1. No ordinary real number does that, so <color=#FFE14D>i</color> brings in a new kind of number. That is what makes α and β complex.

boxes.title: WHY COMPLEX NUMBERS?
boxes.body: Quantum computing needs ℂ² because α and β carry a phase: like arrows, they can add up or cancel out. That interference is what quantum algorithms are built on, and real numbers alone can't describe every state a qubit can be in. You won't need the details in this lesson.

boxes.title: LET'S VISUALIZE IT
boxes.body: Let's try to picture these numbers.

boxes.title: TWO REAL NUMBERS
boxes.body: A pair of real numbers (a, b) is easy to picture: go a steps along x and b steps along y. The arrow from the center to that point is a vector in ℝ², the flat plane you already know. Two real numbers, two directions, one flat picture.

boxes.title: CAN WE DO THE SAME?
boxes.body: ℂ² is also a pair of numbers, (α, β). Can we draw it as an arrow on a flat plane too?
boxes.answer: No. Every complex number already takes two real numbers (a + b<color=#FFE14D>i</color>), so α and β together take four: a, b, c and d. The <color=#FFE14D>i</color> adds a new direction to each one, and a flat plane runs out of room. We need a different kind of picture.

boxes.title: THE BLOCH SPHERE
boxes.body: This is the Bloch sphere, the standard way to picture a qubit's state in quantum computing. Every state is a point on its surface: |0⟩ at the top, |1⟩ at the bottom, and every other state somewhere in between. Why four numbers fit on a sphere takes more advanced math, so we'll take it as given and learn to read it.

boxes.title: WHERE THE QUBIT IS
boxes.body: To show where the qubit is on the Bloch sphere, we use a vector: an arrow from the center to a point on the sphere. This one is |ψ⟩. The vector must be normalized: its length is always exactly 1, the radius of the sphere, so it can never leave the sphere. In terms of α and β, normalized means |α|² + |β|² = 1.

boxes.title: MOVING THE VECTOR
boxes.body: Now, if we want to move this vector, we use special matrices called unitaries. A unitary is an operation that takes a normalized vector to another normalized vector, so the arrow always stays on the sphere.

boxes.title: UNITARIES IN MATH
boxes.body: Applying a unitary U to the state |ψ⟩ is written U|ψ⟩, and it gives a new state |ψ′⟩: the vector just turned from |ψ⟩ (now dim) to |ψ′⟩, still on the sphere. As matrices, U is a 2 × 2 grid of numbers that multiplies the column (α, β) to give the new column (α′, β′). The gates in this lesson are unitaries: on the Bloch sphere, each one turns the vector.
